    12. Completeness of and pointwise convergence#

    We established that the space is a normed vector space for exponents and a quasinormed vector space for . A classical limitation of function spaces such as or that of Riemann integrable functions, equipped with the metric is the failure of metric completeness. For example, Cauchy sequences of continuous functions frequently fail to converge to a continuous limit (Note 1). In a metric or normed space, completeness ensures that every sequence of approximations whose mutual differences shrink to zero converges to an element belonging to the space itself. The primary result of these notes is that is complete for every exponent . Consequently, is a Banach space for every ..

    To establish completeness, it is advantageous to formulate convergence in terms of the -th power functional rather than the norm . Because is expressed directly as an integral of the non-negative pointwise quantity , convergence can be analyzed using the monotone convergence theorem. The proof proceeds in three stages. First, we establish a numerical quasi-triangle inequality with constant and iterate it to bound -th powers of finite sums. Second, we prove that every Cauchy sequence in possesses a subsequence with geometrically decaying consecutive differences, and that convergence of such a subsequence implies convergence of the full Cauchy sequence. Third, for a rapidly Cauchy sequence, we construct the limit pointwise via an absolutely convergent telescoping series and verify that it provides the limit.

    The construction yields a limit function that is simultaneously an limit and an almost-everywhere pointwise limit. In the second half of these notes, we systematically investigate the relationship between convergence in and pointwise convergence almost everywhere. We prove that rapid convergence with summable errors implies almost-everywhere convergence, and we deduce that every -convergent sequence admits an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence. Conversely, we demonstrate through explicit counterexamples (including the typewriter sequence) that neither mode of convergence implies the other in general. Finally, we establish the dominated convergence theorem in , which restores convergence from almost-everywhere convergence under an integrable domination hypothesis.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • State and prove the quasi-triangle inequality for the power functional with constant , and iterate it to bound -th powers of finite sums.

    • Reduce the completeness of to the convergence of rapidly Cauchy sequences with geometrically decaying consecutive differences.

    • Prove the Riesz–Fischer theorem: is complete for every exponent , so that is a Banach space for .

    • Prove that rapid convergence with summable errors implies almost-everywhere convergence, and deduce that every -convergent sequence admits an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence.

    • Construct the typewriter sequence to demonstrate that a sequence can converge in while diverging at every point.

    • Construct sequences showing that almost-everywhere convergence does not imply convergence, both on spaces of infinite measure (escape of mass to infinity) and on spaces of finite measure (concentration of mass).

    • Apply the dominated convergence theorem in to deduce convergence from almost-everywhere convergence under a domination condition.

    Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space, is a fixed exponent, and functions are measurable functions . On subsets of , the symbol denotes Lebesgue measure.

    12.1.2 Reduction to rapidly Cauchy sequences#

    In a general metric space, a Cauchy sequence satisfies the condition that as , but this condition does not specify a rate at which the differences shrink. To construct a candidate limit function as the sum of a telescoping series , we require consecutive differences that decay at a prescribed geometric rate. The next lemma demonstrates that it is sufficient to establish convergence for sequences with geometric decay: every Cauchy sequence admits a subsequence with geometrically decaying differences, and whenever a subsequence of a Cauchy sequence converges, the original Cauchy sequence converges to the same limit.

    Corollary 12.6 ( as a complete space)#

    For , the normed space is complete; a complete normed space is called a Banach space. For , the space equipped with the metric is a complete metric space.

    In particular, is a Banach space. This completeness resolves the failure of completeness of under the metric observed in Note 1: every Cauchy sequence of continuous functions converges in to an element of , even when that limit cannot be represented by any continuous function.

    The proof of Theorem 12.5 established more than convergence in the metric. In Step 2, the rapidly Cauchy sequence was shown to converge to pointwise almost everywhere. Combined with the subsequence extraction in Lemma 12.4, this proves that every Cauchy sequence in possesses a subsequence that converges almost everywhere to its limit. The next section examines this relationship in detail.

    12.3 convergence and pointwise convergence#

    On a measure space , a sequence of functions can approach a limit function in two distinct topological senses:

    1. Pointwise convergence almost everywhere: the numerical sequence converges to for all points outside a set of measure zero.

    2. Convergence in : the integrated average deviation tends to as .

    Convergence in allows to deviate substantially from on sets of small measure, provided the total integral remains small. In this section, we determine the precise connection between these two modes of convergence.

    While convergence in alone does not imply pointwise convergence everywhere, convergence with summable errors ensures convergence almost everywhere.

    12.3.3 Pointwise convergence without convergence#

    Conversely, a sequence of functions may converge pointwise almost everywhere to a limit function without converging in the metric. Two distinct analytical mechanisms produce this behavior: the escape of mass to infinity on spaces of infinite measure, and the concentration of mass on shrinking sets.

    12.3.4 Domination restores convergence#

    In our study of integral limit theorems (Note 22), the dominated convergence theorem prevented both escape of mass to infinity and mass concentration by requiring a single dominating integrable function. Applying that theorem to the power difference establishes that almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence whenever the sequence is dominated in .

    Remark (Summary of relations between and almost-everywhere convergence)#

    For and functions :

    • Rapid convergence implies almost-everywhere convergence: If , then almost everywhere (Theorem 12.7).

    • Subsequential convergence: If in , then a subsequence converges to almost everywhere (Corollary 12.8), although the full sequence may converge at no point (Example 12.10).

    • Pointwise convergence does not imply convergence: Almost-everywhere convergence does not guarantee convergence, even on a space of finite measure (Example 12.11); however, convergence is restored when the sequence is dominated by a function in (Proposition 12.12).

    • Consistency of limits: Whenever a sequence converges both in and almost everywhere, the two limits coincide almost everywhere (Corollary 12.9).
